newsitem.title: USA: Komag says Q4 EPS to be below Q3's $0.31/shr.
newsitem.headline: Komag says Q4 EPS to be below Q3's $0.31/shr.

text.p: Komag Inc, a supplier of thin-film media for computer hard disk drives, said on Monday its results for the fourth quarter ending December 29 will fall below its results reported for the third quarter.

It previously said earnings per share for the fourth quarter would be higher than the $0.31 per share in the third quarter of 1996 but likely below the $0.72 per share recorded in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Komag now said the company's earnings per share for the fourth quarter will fall below the results of the third quarter of 1996.

Komag said unit production output for the fourth quarter will not meet its targeted level due to lower-than-expected manufacturing yields on its new product offerings. The lower production level will constrain net sales and adversely affect unit production costs for the fourth quarter, it said.
It said fourth quarter gross margins will fall below third quarter levels. It previously forecast gross margin percentage to improve over the 24 percent recorded in the third quarter.
Nevertheless, startup of production on two new production lines during the quarter should increase unit output above the 10.7 million disks in the third quarter, it said.
The higher production level and a cut in its finished goods inventory should result in higher fourth quarter net sales relative to third quarter sales of $131.5 million.

Komag previously said fourth quarter net sales should surpass the $152 million level reported for the first and second quarters of 1996. It now expects fourth quarter sales to exceed third quarter sales but fall short of $152 million.

It previously said fiscal 1996 results to compare favorably to fiscal 1995. But it said now that the weak performances in the fourth quarter may cause earnings per share for the 1996 fiscal year to fall below the $2.14 per share posted in fiscal 1995.
Earnings for the first nine months of 1996 totalled $1.91 per share.

"While we remain confident in the abilities of our concurrent engineering teams to solve these yield-related issues, the rate at which we improve yields on these demanding new products will likely be slower than our historical rate of improvement. As a result, our financial performance will likely remain constrained during the first half of 1997," said Stephen Johnson, president and chief executive officer.
